name: Philosophical Skepticism
statement: We cannot know what we ordinarily claim to know: doubt raised to a philosophical principle.
statementAccent: doubt raised to a philosophical principle
meaning: Philosophical skepticism is the view, or family of views, that questions or denies our ability to have knowledge, or justified or certain belief, in some or all domains. It is distinct from ordinary, everyday doubt: the philosophical skeptic argues that we do not know propositions we ordinarily take ourselves to know, such as that there is an external world, that other minds exist, or that the future will resemble the past. Skepticism comes in different scopes. Global or radical skepticism denies that we have knowledge or justified belief about any proposition, while local skepticism is restricted to a domain, such as Cartesian skepticism about the external world or Humean skepticism about what we infer by non-deductive, inductive reasoning. It also comes in different traditions. Ancient Academic skepticism, in the skeptical phase of Plato's Academy under figures such as Arcesilaus and Carneades, held that knowledge in the strong Stoic sense is impossible. Pyrrhonian skepticism, deriving from Pyrrho and systematized by Sextus Empiricus, proceeds by opposing arguments of equal force to reach suspension of judgment, without dogmatically asserting that knowledge is impossible. Modern Cartesian skepticism uses radical doubt, the dreaming argument and the evil demon, methodically, as a tool to seek an indubitable foundation. Skepticism is a driving force in epistemology, setting the challenge that theories of knowledge exist to answer.
mechanism: Philosophical skepticism works by constructing arguments that our ordinary beliefs fall short of knowledge or justification, and different skepticisms use different engines. A central device is the skeptical hypothesis: a scenario, such as that one is now dreaming, or is being deceived by an evil demon, or is a brain in a vat, in which one would have exactly the experiences one actually has yet one's ordinary beliefs would be false. Because experience alone cannot distinguish the ordinary situation from the skeptical scenario, the argument concludes that one does not know the ordinary beliefs to be true. A related form uses a closure principle: if knowing something requires knowing what it entails, and one cannot know that one is not a brain in a vat, then one cannot know the everyday propositions that entail it. Other engines are older. Agrippa's trilemma, or the regress problem, urges that any attempted justification must either regress infinitely, argue in a circle, or stop arbitrarily at an unjustified assumption. The problem of the criterion argues that to identify knowledge one needs a criterion, yet validating the criterion presupposes one already knows the cases, a circle. Hume's problem of induction argues that inference from observed to unobserved cannot be justified without circularity. Pyrrhonism assembles such oppositions to induce equipollence, a balance of reasons for and against, leading to suspension of judgment, from which, Sextus says, tranquility unexpectedly follows.

examples.text: Since dreaming can be subjectively indistinguishable from waking, the skeptic asks how you can be certain you are not now dreaming.

examples.tag: The evil demon and the vat
examples.text: A systematically deceived brain in a vat would have experiences identical to yours, so experience cannot rule the scenario out.
The Pyrrhonist opposes arguments of equal force to reach suspension of judgment rather than asserting that knowledge is impossible.

variants.name: Global versus local
variants.text: Radical skepticism about all propositions, versus local skepticism about a domain such as the external world or induction.

variants.name: Academic versus Pyrrhonian
variants.text: Academic skeptics asserted knowledge is impossible; Pyrrhonists suspended judgment without asserting even that.

whyItMatters: Philosophical skepticism is one of the great engines of the theory of knowledge, the challenge against which epistemology has defined itself for over two thousand years. By arguing that we do not know even the things we are most confident of, that there is an external world, that the sun will rise, that other people have minds, the skeptic forces us to ask what knowledge really requires and whether we can meet the standard. The history of epistemology is in large part a series of responses to skepticism: Descartes's cogito as an indubitable foundation surviving radical doubt, Moore's common-sense insistence that he knows he has hands, contextualism's claim that knowledge ascriptions shift with the standards in play, the relevant-alternatives view that one need only rule out relevant possibilities, and Putnam's argument that the brain-in-a-vat hypothesis is self-refuting. The distinctions skepticism forces, between method and doctrine, global and local, Academic and Pyrrhonian, sharpen our grip on knowledge and justification. Skepticism also disciplines dogmatism, reminding us how much of what we believe outruns what we can conclusively prove. As doubt raised to a principle and pressed with rigor, philosophical skepticism is the permanent provocation at the heart of epistemology.

working.text: question beliefs we take for granted, such as that there is an external world or that induction is reliable.
use a skeptical hypothesis, the regress trilemma, the criterion problem, or the problem of induction to undercut justification.
conclude that we lack knowledge, or, in Pyrrhonism, suspend judgment rather than assert impossibility.

limits: Philosophical skepticism faces the perennial charge of self-refutation and a range of anti-skeptical replies, and its own varieties differ over how to avoid the charge. If a skeptic claims to know that knowledge is impossible, the claim undermines itself, which is precisely why the Pyrrhonist suspends judgment and remains investigating rather than asserting impossibility, unlike the Academic skeptic who states a doctrine. Modern responses attack the skeptical arguments directly: contextualists hold that skeptical scenarios only raise the standard for knowledge in special contexts, so ordinary knowledge claims remain true in ordinary contexts; relevant-alternatives theorists, following Dretske, hold that one need only rule out relevant alternatives, not every logically possible one, and may deny the closure principle the skeptic relies on; and semantic externalists, following Putnam, argue that the very hypothesis we are brains in a vat is self-refuting when uttered, since a vat-brain's words would not refer to real vats, though this is a metalinguistic result that does not by itself prove we are not envatted. Skepticism is thus better seen as a family of challenges than as an established conclusion. So philosophical skepticism robustly presses the limits of knowledge, understood as a set of arguments answered variously by foundationalism, contextualism, relevant alternatives, and externalism, and dogged by the self-refutation worry.
misreadings: Philosophical skepticism is not mere everyday doubt about particular claims; it questions whether we can know things we ordinarily take ourselves to know at all. It is not a single thesis, since global and local, Academic and Pyrrhonian, and methodological and doctrinal skepticisms differ importantly, and the Pyrrhonist does not even assert that knowledge is impossible. And Cartesian doubt is not skepticism embraced for its own sake but a method to reach an indubitable foundation, so treating skepticism as ordinary doubt, as one uniform doctrine, or as Descartes's final position, misreads a family of challenges central to epistemology.
origin: A family of philosophical views questioning or denying knowledge or justified belief, ranging from ancient Academic and Pyrrhonian skepticism through Cartesian and Humean skepticism to modern debates over external-world knowledge.
